Article Title: Punjab: 'Khedan Wattan Punjab Diyan' begins from Bathinda
Article Text:
Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann setting a vision of taking the state's sporting talent to the global stage.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bathinda, Punjab's sports event, 'Khedan Wattan Punjab Diyan-2026', began on Saturday, with Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann setting a vision of taking the state's sporting talent to the global stage.The fourth season will bring nearly 10 lakh players aged 14 to over 70 years into 39 sporting disciplines, including four para-sports.The event, which kicked off in Bathinda, will conclude in Patiala on November 29, with Rs 12.50 crore in prize money for winners, including cash awards for veteran players for the first time, according to an official statement.On the occasion, Mann also honoured Commonwealth Games-2026 silver medallists Harjinder Kaur and Lovepreet Singh with Rs 50 lakh each.The opening ceremony of the fourth season of the Games featured several performances, including Bhangra and Giddha. Legendary Punjabi artist Gurdas Maan and Kulwinder Billa also performed at the ceremony.Announcing the Games open at Shaheed Bhagat Singh Stadium, Mann said, "We are known for our valour, enterprise and sporting spirit, due to which we have always excelled in every field. These games aim at channelising this spirit and providing our youth with a platform to excel in sports.""For the first time, tennis-ball cricket for boys and girls has also been included as a demonstration sport," the CM said."Khedan Wattan Punjab Diyan is the best platform for identifying, nurturing and polishing hidden sporting talent from every corner of Punjab's villages and cities," said CM Bhagwant Singh Mann, adding that the state government is committed to preparing children for competitions at national and international levels.For the first time, veteran athletes will also be felicitated with cash prizes."State-level gold medal winners will receive Rs 10,000, silver medal winners Rs 7,000 and bronze medal winners Rs 5,000. Medal-winning athletes up to 40 years of age will also receive grading certificates, enabling them to avail the benefits of the sports quota in government jobs," he added.Mann said under the New Sports Policy, financial assistance is also being provided to athletes for preparation for major competitions.Fifteen lakh rupees is being provided for Olympic preparation and Rs 8 lakh for preparation for the Asian and Commonwealth Games. So far, Rs 15 crore has been distributed to athletes for training and preparation.On sports infrastructure, Mann said 3,148 rural sports grounds are being developed across the state, of which 750 have already been inaugurated."Six thousand gyms are being established, with 500 already dedicated to the people in the first phase. Rs 12.50 crore had been transferred directly into the bank accounts of 9,501 athletes for purchasing sports equipment," he added.
Article Summary: Chief minister bhagwant mann setting a vision of taking the state's sporting talent to the global stage. The fourth season will bring nearly 10 lakh players aged 14 to over 70 years into 39 sporting disciplines, including four para-sports. The event, which kicked off in bathinda, will conclude in patiala on november 29.

Gold, the second biggest import item for India in terms of value, is increasingly playing an important role in the circular economy that can meet part of the demand for the yellow metal from internal sources and save precious foreign exchange reserves. To integrate gold into the circular economy, every stakeholder is stepping up to bring in more transparency, trust, purity and responsible mining practices, experts from the field said.The panel consisted of Asher O, MD – India Operations, Malabar Gold & Diamonds; Sachin Jain, Regional CEO India, World Gold Council; Vikram Dhawan, Head Commodities and Fund Manager, Nippon India Mutual Fund, Kaushlendra Sinha, CEO, Indian Association for Gold Excellence and Standards; and Mayank Sharma, President and Head of Gold Loan, IIFL Finance.Asher said Malabar Gold & Diamonds meets about 80% of the demand for gold from people trading in their old stock. Sinha of IAGES said a recent study by the entity showed a large number of young buyers were asking about gold’s source, indicating a responsible buying attitude. Jain of WGC said they released a report suggesting responsible mining in India to substitute excessive dependence on imports. Sharma discussed gold loans and how credit flow from the sector is helping households and MSMEs. Dhawan explained how gold ETFs are leading to financialisation of the metal.tnn

Article Title: ‘Scared to work’: Ex-Pakistan cricketer opens up on Mohsin Naqvi-led PCB
Article Text:
Chairman of Pakistan Cricket Board Mohsin Naqvi, centre, chats with Pakistan's Babar Azam, left, as head coach Mike Hesson watches (AP Photo)

Mushtaq reveals why he is hesitant

'This is not the right thing'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

PCB under growing scrutiny

The Pakistan Cricket Board’s decision to overhaul the national team in the middle of its England tour continues to face scrutiny, with former Pakistan spinner Mushtaq Ahmed admitting that the uncertainty surrounding coaching positions has made him wary of taking up a role with the national side.A week after the PCB sent seven players and two coaches back to Pakistan, the fallout from the decision remains a major talking point. The board has frequently faced criticism for making repeated changes to its coaches and captains, and Mushtaq believes that the lack of stability is now becoming a deterrent for former players who want to serve Pakistan in coaching roles.The PCB took the drastic step after Pakistan suffered heavy defeats in the opening two Tests against England. Mohammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq and Salman Ali Agha were among the players sent home, while Sarfaraz Ahmed and Umar Gul were also removed from the coaching setup. They were replaced in the dressing room by Mike Hesson and Ashley Noffke.Mushtaq was asked whether he would be interested in coaching Pakistan and made it clear that he would welcome the chance to work with the national team. However, he also explained why the current environment leaves him concerned about accepting such a responsibility.The former spinner pointed to the treatment of coaches and the possibility of being removed abruptly, even while a tour is still in progress.“I would love to do that for my country, of course. Especially at this time.Obviously, I need only one thing. Sometimes you get scared of working for your own country when the people don’t respect you, and they sack you because of a few emotional decisions here and there. When you see those things, people getting sacked on a tour, you get worried and scared,” Mushtaq said on the BBC Stumped Podcast.Despite his concerns, Mushtaq believes there is an opportunity for Pakistani coaches to make a meaningful contribution if greater stability can be established within the system.“I think those are the things that if you can get that sorted, I think every Pakistani cricketer who is coaching, not only myself, they’d love to serve the country. This is the best time for me to take that challenge and bring those players to their best, make them confident about international cricket and make a unit that can actually challenge opposition teams,” he added.Mushtaq also strongly disagreed with the PCB's decision to make such sweeping changes while the England series was still underway.The former Pakistan international, who played 52 Tests and 144 ODIs, questioned the rationale behind sending seven players home and altering the coaching staff midway through an overseas tour.“Changing seven players and the management, especially with the tour still going on, I feel that this is not the right thing,” Mushtaq said.He was particularly critical of the timing of the decision involving Sarfaraz and Umar Gul, arguing that changes of this magnitude should have been considered after the completion of the tour.“This has never happened in Pakistan cricket before. Obviously, I’m hurt as an ex-cricketer, as a Pakistani, these things should not happen. Sarfaraz and Umar Gul, they are some of the most experienced cricketers. They serve the country very well. Sarfaraz was a captain also. If you want to sack them, obviously, you have to sack them after the tour. This is the time to stay calm, don’t make rash decisions," he added.The mid-tour shake-up has attracted criticism beyond Pakistan, with Michael Atherton, Nasser Hussain and Jason Gillespie among those who have questioned the PCB's decision.The board's changes came after Pakistan's disappointing results in the first two Tests, leaving the team facing the prospect of a difficult end to the tour.Pakistan will now look to finish the series on a positive note when they face England in the third and final Test, beginning on September 9 in Birmingham. However, with questions over the board's approach to coaches, players and decision-making continuing to mount, the debate surrounding Pakistan cricket is unlikely to end with the conclusion of the Test series.
Article Summary: Mushtaq ahmed reveals why he is hesitant to take up a coaching role with the pakistan national side. The former spinner believes that the uncertainty surrounding coaching positions has made him wary of taking up a role. Mushtaq also strongly disagreed with the pcb's decision to make such sweeping changes while the england series was still underway.

Article Title: Who was Bill Dundee? Wrestling legend and Jerry "The King" Lawler’s longtime friend passes away at 82
Article Text:
Bill Dundee. Image via: Memphis Wrestling/ YouTube

Who was Bill Dundee?

Bill Dundee dies at 82, family and WWE react

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bill Dundee's wrestling legacy

Bill Dundee spent more than half a century inside wrestling rings across three continents, and somehow his final on-camera moment landed just one day before his death. That kind of timing doesn't happen by design, but it's exactly how Memphis wrestling said goodbye to one of its own.Dundee died early Sunday morning at 82. His son, Jamie Dundee, broke the news, and within hours tributes started pouring in from a wrestling world that had watched Dundee build his legacy over five decades.Bill Dundee was born William Cruickshanks in Scotland and grew up in Australia, where his path into wrestling started in an unlikely place. As a teenager, he joined a circus and worked as a trapeze artist before ever stepping into a ring. He began wrestling professionally in Australia in the late 1960s and arrived in the United States in 1974.Memphis became his home base, and his career there became inseparable from Jerry "The King" Lawler. The two spent years shifting between fierce rivals and championship-winning partners, and their matches, built around elaborate stipulations and personal feuds, turned into some of the most memorable moments in Memphis wrestling history.Dundee also worked behind the scenes as a booker in several territories, a role that shaped the business as much as his in-ring work did.Jamie Dundee announced his father's death on Facebook early Sunday, saying he died at around 3:30 a.m. and signing off, "Bill's Boy." No cause of death has been made public. Jamie had previously revealed that his father was living with stage three dementia, though nothing has tied that diagnosis to his death.WWE released a statement Sunday afternoon, writing that it was "saddened to learn that Memphis wrestling legend Bill Dundee has passed away," and extended condolences to his family and fans.Just a day earlier, Memphis Wrestling aired what turned out to be Dundee's final televised appearance, recorded before it aired Saturday on WMC. Current roster members lined up to shake his hand as announcer Dustin Starr recalled his championship battles with Lawler.Nobody watching knew it would double as a farewell.Dundee held the AWA Southern Heavyweight Championship nine times and the CWA International Heavyweight Championship four times, and alongside Lawler, he won the AWA World Tag Team Championship twice, including a run that began in October 1987. Their most famous feud, in 1977, carried hair stipulations and even Lawler's Cadillac as a wager.He was inducted into the Memphis Wrestling Hall of Fame in 2017, sharing the stage with Lawler, Jimmy Hart, and Koko B. Ware. Dundee kept wrestling well past his prime years, taking his final match in December 2019, nearly 45 years after he first landed in Memphis. He also spent time in WCW under the name Sir William, managing Steven Regal.
Article Summary: Memphis wrestling legend bill dundee has died at 82. Dundee was inducted into the memphis wrestling hall of fame in 2017. His son, jamie dundee, announced his father's death on facebook. No cause of death has been made public.

Article Title: Trophy controversy returns? Mohsin Naqvi set to attend India’s Women’s Asia Cup final
Article Text:
Indian Men's Cricket Team and Mohsin Naqvi

Trophy drama could return

What happened in last year's final?

Why would Naqvi present the trophy?

India dominate Women's Asia Cup campaign

Poll Vote & Share your view Should India accept the trophy from Mohsin Naqvi if they win the Asia Cup? Yes, it’s about sportsmanship No, due to past controversies Only if there are assurances of goodwill It doesn't matter, win is what counts 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The possibility of another trophy presentation controversy involving India and Pakistan has emerged ahead of the ACC Women’s Asia Cup 2026 final, with Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) chairman and Asian Cricket Council (ACC) president Mohsin Naqvi set to attend the summit clash in Dubai.According to a Geo Super report, Naqvi is expected to be the chief guest at the closing ceremony of the tournament on September 13. His presence could once again bring the focus on the trophy presentation if Harmanpreet Kaur’s India reach the final and go on to win the title.Naqvi was at the centre of a major controversy during last year's Men's Asia Cup final at the Dubai International Stadium. India defeated Pakistan in the summit clash but refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi, who was the ACC president and also PCB chairman.The episode took place against a particularly tense backdrop. The Men's Asia Cup was played after the Pahalgam terror attack, while Naqvi had also shared anti-India statements on social media during the tournament in his capacity as Pakistan's Interior Minister.With Naqvi expected to attend the Women's Asia Cup final, another trophy-related standoff could potentially unfold.If India win the tournament, Naqvi could be the official presenting the silverware to the champions because of his position as ACC president.The decision on whether to accept it from him, however, would ultimately rest with the Harmanpreet-led Indian team.The BCCI has so far remained silent on what the women's side would do if they win the tournament and Naqvi is present for the presentation.India are among the favourites for the title and have already secured their place in the semi-finals without losing a match. They made a particularly strong statement against Pakistan, defeating the Fatima Sana-led side by seven wickets after bowling them out for just 55 in Dubai.The controversy involving Naqvi began after India defeated Pakistan in the Men's Asia Cup final on September 28, 2025.The Suryakumar Yadav-led Indian side completed the victory, but the post-match presentation was delayed by more than an hour as discussions continued over who would present the trophy.India eventually chose not to receive the silverware from Naqvi. The players celebrated their title triumph on the podium without the trophy, while Naqvi left the stadium with it.The Asia Cup trophy has still not been handed over to India and remains at the ACC office in Dubai.The situation became one of the most talked-about moments of the tournament, particularly because Naqvi had attended the final despite the earlier tensions between the two sides.Naqvi holds two key positions relevant to the presentation. He is the PCB chairman as well as the president of the ACC.Since the Women's Asia Cup is an ACC-hosted tournament, Naqvi, by virtue of his position as ACC president, holds the right to present the trophy to the winners.That means another India-Pakistan trophy moment could be waiting in Dubai if Harmanpreet Kaur's team reaches the final and lifts the title.India have been unbeaten throughout their campaign in the eight-team Women's Asia Cup. Harmanpreet Kaur's side began the tournament with a victory over Thailand before producing convincing wins against Hong Kong and Pakistan in the group stage.The tournament has also witnessed a major individual milestone for Smriti Mandhana, who became the leading run-scorer in women's international cricket after surpassing former India captain Mithali Raj.With India already through to the semi-finals, attention will now turn to the knockout stage. If the Women in Blue make it all the way to the final and win the trophy on September 13, Naqvi's presence could set the stage for another closely watched presentation ceremony in Dubai.

Article Title: ‘Men would never have to face this’: Keyaa Banerji calls out sexism after viral 140kg deadlift and World Championship silver
Article Text:
21-year-old Keyaa Banerji (Image Source: X)

ALSO READ:

A medal, a viral lift and an uncomfortable spotlight

‘I was aiming to break the Asian record’

‘It’s always something I really enjoyed’

More than just lifting heavy weights

Looking beyond the online noise

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Indian powerlifter Keyaa Kunal Banerji had every reason to expect attention after producing one of the standout performances of her young career. Instead, the 21-year-old found herself confronting an uncomfortable side of online fame after her 140kg deadlift and World Championship silver medal went viral.Banerji's breakthrough came at the 2026 IPF World Sub-Junior and Junior Classic Powerlifting Championships in Sun City, South Africa, where she competed in the Junior Women's 47kg category. Weighing 45.70kg, she pulled 140kg in the deadlift — more than three times her competition bodyweight — to finish second in the individual deadlift event and win a silver medal.But as the clip of her lift spread across social media, much of the conversation around her achievement shifted away from powerlifting. Banerji said she was subjected to trolling, fake accounts, misuse of her images and thousands of unauthorised AI-generated manipulated images using her likeness.For the young athlete, the experience was not simply about unpleasant comments. She saw it as a stark example of the sexism women athletes continue to encounter when their achievements attract a large online audience."I think it was just sexism at its finest. I don't think I can put it any other way.The way I was treated - men would never have to face this, like after winning a championship or something like that; a male athlete never has to face something like this," Banerji told ANI."Most of the conversation revolved around my appearance. All people would talk about was my appearance, and I think that really bothered me because I had accomplished something so big for myself and I had done something so big in my sport," she added.The irony was not lost on Banerji. The lift that drew widespread attention was itself the product of years of work and a sport that she has come to deeply enjoy.At the World Championships, Banerji also recorded a 90kg squat and a 50kg bench press, finishing with a 280kg total and placing fifth overall in the Junior Women's 47kg category. France's Ines Herbaux won the individual deadlift gold with 165kg, while Ireland's Blathnaid O'Dwyer also lifted 140kg.Banerji, however, had arrived at the competition with ambitions that went beyond simply making the podium."I think initially it is a great feeling. Once it came out on social media, I did get a little bit overwhelmed. There was some negative attention, but I would like to avoid talking about that too much. I am very proud of myself and very happy with my accomplishment. I have been working towards this for two years," she said.The silver medal itself had not been part of her original expectations."This silver medal was something I wasn't expecting initially. I was just happy to be present at the World Championship because powerlifting is a long-term sport. I do have plans of eventually winning a World Championship and getting a gold back for the country," Banerji said."It started with me thinking that this World Championship is something I'm going to attend just for experience. The fact that I ended up putting such a good number up and winning a medal was just absolutely incredible," she added.The 140kg deadlift became the defining moment of her campaign, but Banerji's own assessment of the lift was more measured. She explained that competition-day performances can differ considerably from what an athlete manages in training."Competition day numbers and training numbers aren't always the same. Performing as an athlete on competition day is very different from what you do in training. In powerlifting, we usually try to hit maxes in competition," she said."Although my result worked out in a way that I won a silver medal, as an athlete, the planning that my coach and I had done, 140 kg was on the lower end of the range for what we were planning to hit that day," she added.In training, Banerji had already gone beyond that mark."In training, I have hit around 147.5 kg and 150 kg several times. 147.5 kg is also the Asian record. So, my ideal day would have been breaking the Asian record on stage. I was a little disheartened that I wasn't able to do that," she said.The 140kg lift was only her second deadlift attempt. She subsequently went for 142.5kg but could not complete it."140 kg wasn't my third deadlift; it was my second deadlift. It moved a little bit slower than expected compared to how it moves in training. So, I took a smaller jump of 142.5 after that, and I failed that lift. It wasn't an ideal day, but things worked out," she said.While the online attention was difficult, Banerji does not want the trolling to define the story of her World Championship campaign."In fact, I'm really grateful for the opportunity to be talking to news channels because it gives me the opportunity to actually talk about my passion for the sport and my journey progressing my numbers, etc. So, I'm over it. I'm definitely over it. But it was a little bit hard in the middle," she said.That passion dates back to when powerlifting was not even part of her plans."When I was first starting out, I just started going to the gym for a sense of personal fulfilment and just taking care of my health, etc. But I had a friend who was a powerlifting coach and was also competing at a world level. He has also won a gold medal for the country. So, I felt extremely inspired and felt very curious about how this works," she said.That curiosity eventually became competitive ambition as her numbers improved in the squat, bench press and deadlift.Banerji also stressed that powerlifting is a highly technical discipline, contrary to the simplistic perception that it is merely about lifting as much weight as possible."There are rules, making sure that your lift matches the commands of the referee, making sure that once you've picked up, for instance, once you've completed your deadlift, you can't just leave the bar. You can only put it down once the referee asks you to put it down. So, there are a lot of, it's a very technical sport. There are a lot of things that go into it," she said.For Banerji, the sport has also been a constant through an important period of her life."My sport is something that really helped me in my life. During my college times, I used to look forward to training. Sometimes I would have to train at night, sometimes I would have to skip classes to train, but it's something that never really bothered me. It's always something I really enjoyed," she said.Her progression is reflected in her numbers. At the 2025 National Championship, she lifted 82.5kg in the squat, 47.5kg in the bench press and 127.5kg in the deadlift for a 257.5kg total. She later improved to 95kg in the squat, 52.5kg in the bench press and 140kg in the deadlift, taking her total to 287.5kg.The World Championship therefore represented another significant step, even if her own assessment suggests there is considerably more to come."I can't explain it, and I am overwhelmed. I was very happy to just be there. To be at that World Championship, meet my competitors, see the girls that I used to look up to around me and compete in the same competition — it was an unreal feeling," she said.Banerji, who recently graduated from Ashoka University with a BSc in Psychology, is considering pursuing an MBA. But her immediate sporting ambition remains clear: continue improving her numbers and eventually win a World Championship gold for India.The unwanted online attention may have become part of her story, but it is not what Banerji wants to be remembered for.
Article Summary: Keyaa kunal banerji, 21, won a silver medal at the 2026 ipf world sub-junior and junior classic powerlifting championships in south africa. She pulled 140kg in the deadlift, more than three times her competition bodyweight. But as the clip of her lift spread across social media, much of the conversation around her achievement shifted away from powerlifting.

Article Title: ‘This is not sustainable’: US Open’s post-2 am finishes spark player backlash as Navratilova, Becker question late-night scheduling
Article Text:
Matches increasingly spill into the early hours at US Open 2026. (Pic credit: X/AP)

‘Everybody wants to go to sleep’

Alexander Zverev of Germany (AP Photo)

Pegula questions whether it is ‘the right thing’

Jessica Pegula of the United States (AP Photo)

Venus Williams caught in historic late start

Shelton experiences his first 2 am finish

Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus (AP Photo)

Sabalenka warns of disrupted schedules

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The US Open’s famous late-night energy is once again coming under scrutiny, but this time the concern is not about whether New York can keep the party going. It is about whether the players can.As the first week of the Grand Slam winds down, a growing number of matches have stretched well past midnight, with three of the first six night sessions finishing after 2 am (local time) and two others extending beyond 1 am. The unusually late endings have prompted four-time US Open singles champion Martina Navratilova , six-time Grand Slam winner Boris Becker and several players to question whether the scheduling has gone too far.Navratilova was among the most direct in her criticism, posting on X after the tournament recorded three post-2 am finishes in its opening six days."This is not sustainable…": Navratilova wrote while sharing statistics highlighting the late finishes.Becker, the 1989 US Open champion, also weighed in after Navratilova's post, questioning why tennis players are being asked to compete at such hours."That’s simple to late to play tennis ?? anymore….tell me another sport like that ?!?," Becker posted.The issue has become particularly noticeable in a tournament where night tennis has long been part of its identity.Arthur Ashe Stadium under the lights, packed stands and an electric New York crowd are among the defining images of the US Open. But as matches increasingly spill into the early hours, players and former champions are beginning to question where the line should be drawn.Alexander Zverev had little appetite for an extended discussion after his first-round match ended in the early hours. With empty seats visible around the court, the German top seed took just two questions from reporters before making his feelings clear."I think everybody's tired," he said. "Everybody wants to go to sleep."The problem became even more pronounced for Zverev as the tournament progressed. His first two matches finished at 1:55 am and 2:15 am, respectively, making him the first top-seeded man to play back-to-back five-set matches to begin a major in the Open era, which dates back to 1968.His experience has underlined the physical cost of the scheduling, particularly when players have to recover from long matches and then prepare for the next round within a limited window.Third-ranked women's player Jessica Pegula acknowledged that tournament organisers have to balance several competing demands, including television schedules and match timings. But she questioned whether those considerations should come at the expense of players having to compete deep into the night."I know they're dealing with a lot of different aspects as far as broadcast and TV and making sure certain matches get done and are starting at a certain time for those reasons," Pegula said."But you have to wonder if it's really the right thing for players to be finishing at 2 am, especially when it’s not — like, I'm not watching on TV. I'm sleeping. Some people stay, but there is a lot of people that need to go home."Her comments reflect a broader concern around the sustainability of the current schedule. A late finish does not simply mean a player leaves the court later. It can affect meals, recovery, sleep and preparation for the following day.Other Grand Slam tournaments have taken different approaches. Wimbledon has instituted an 11 pm curfew, while the French Open schedules only one match during its night session.The US Open, meanwhile, has traditionally embraced the possibility of matches running deep into the night. This year's schedule, however, has pushed that tradition to an extreme.The issue was apparent from the opening night itself.Novak Djokovic's first-round match lasted four hours and 36 minutes on August 30. The length of that contest pushed Venus Williams and Sofia Kenin onto court at 12:13 am, the latest match start in US Open history.Much of the crowd stayed to watch what could have been the 46-year-old Williams' final Grand Slam singles match. But the timing made the occasion more difficult for both players."It's not ideal," Williams said. "I would have preferred something else, definitely. It wasn't great for either of us, so I think we both tried our best. I just don't know any other sport where you have to start that late. I definitely think there's room for improvement there."The match eventually concluded at 2:01 am, adding another chapter to a tournament already seeing an unusual number of after-midnight finishes.Ben Shelton also found himself dealing with the consequences of the scheduling when his second-round match against Denis Shapovalov, which began on Friday night, finished at 2:07 am Saturday.The delay was partly caused by the Williams sisters' doubles match, which lasted more than three hours."Not easy," Shelton said after defeating Shapovalov in 3 hours, 22 minutes. "My first time experiencing playing this late."Shelton estimated that he would not get to sleep until around 5 am, highlighting how a match that ends after 2 am can effectively consume much of the following morning as well.Four of the 17 latest finishes in US Open history have now occurred this year. The tournament record remains 2:50 am, set in 2022 when Carlos Alcaraz defeated Jannik Sinner in the quarterfinals on his way to his first US Open title.Top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka, who two years ago played what was then the fourth-latest women's match in tournament history, has also experienced the knock-on effects of finishing after midnight.She is not a fan of such late starts and the disruption they can cause to an athlete's routine."When you finish late, the next day shifts a lot," Sabalenka said. "Like, you still need to get your hours of sleep, so you start later. You just can really mess up your schedule."That is at the heart of the debate surrounding the US Open's night sessions. The spectacle of late-night tennis can be a major attraction for fans, broadcasters and the tournament itself. But for the athletes, a match finishing at 2 am can have consequences that extend well beyond the final point.With four of the latest 17 finishes in tournament history already coming this year, the question is no longer simply whether New York's tennis nights can continue deep into the morning.It is whether they should.For Navratilova, the answer appears increasingly clear: "This is not sustainable…".
Article Summary: Matches increasingly spill into the early hours at us open 2026. Three of the first six night sessions finished after 2 am (local time) and two others extended beyond 1 am. The unusually late endings have prompted several players to question whether the scheduling has gone too far.

Carlos Alcaraz’s rise to seven Grand Slam titles has been shaped by more than his talent on the tennis court. A lesson from his grandfather, Carlos Alcaraz Lerma, became one of the most personal parts of his career: “Cabeza, corazón y cojones” - head, heart and courage. Alcaraz later had the three Cs tattooed on his wrist as a reminder of that message. His close relationship with former world No. 1 Juan Carlos Ferrero also played a major role in his development. Together, those family and coaching ties helped shape the player who became the youngest man to complete the Career Grand Slam in 2026.The phrase came from Alcaraz’s grandfather and stayed with him as he grew up in El Palmar, Murcia. The three words are “Cabeza, corazón y cojones”, which mean head, heart and courage, with the final Spanish word being a much stronger and more informal expression.For Alcaraz, the idea was simple. He needed his head to make the right decisions, his heart to play with passion and courage to take risks when the pressure was highest.Alcaraz has spoken about the message before, saying:“My grandfather always told me to focus on the Three Cs: head, heart, and balls.”The words became closely linked with his identity as a player. His tennis is built around attacking shots, quick movement and a willingness to try difficult plays even when a match is going against him.The story also has a strong family connection. Alcaraz’s grandfather was involved with tennis in El Palmar, where the young player spent part of his early years around the sport.That makes the “Three Cs” more than a slogan. It is a piece of advice that Alcaraz has carried from his childhood into the biggest matches of his career.After breaking through at the highest level, Alcaraz chose to keep his grandfather’s message with him permanently. In 2022, he got a CCC tattoo, representing “Cabeza, Corazón y Cojones.”The tattoo became a visible reminder of the words that had followed him through his early tennis career. Reports at the time said the tattoo was placed on his wrist and was connected directly to his grandfather’s motto.The timing was also significant. Alcaraz had just enjoyed the breakthrough season that changed his career. He won his first Masters 1000 title in Miami in April 2022 and then won his first Grand Slam at the US Open later that year.By September 2022, he had also become the youngest player to reach No. 1 in the ATP rankings at 19 years and four months. He finished that season as the youngest year-end No. 1 in ATP history.The tattoo therefore came during the period when Alcaraz was moving from a highly rated teenager to one of the biggest names in tennis.Rather than choosing a trophy or a tournament date, he picked something tied to his family.Alcaraz’s grandfather gave him the message, but Juan Carlos Ferrero became one of the most important people in turning that young talent into a top-level player.Ferrero, a former world No. 1 and 2003 French Open champion, began working with Alcaraz when the Spaniard was a teenager. Alcaraz trained at Ferrero’s academy in Villena, Spain, and their relationship grew far beyond normal coach-player duties.Alcaraz has openly described Ferrero as his mentor and second father.“He was my mentor. Everything that I’ve done is thanks to him. I learned a lot, not only professionally, but the personal part as well. He’s my second father… I am the person and the player I am today thanks to him.”Those comments came after years of working together. Ferrero also described Alcaraz as being like a fourth child to him, showing how close the relationship had become.One of the most emotional moments in their relationship came in 2022. Ferrero’s father, Eduardo Ferrero, died suddenly in March while Juan Carlos was in the United States with Alcaraz. Ferrero returned to Spain for the funeral before coming back to Miami, where Alcaraz was preparing for the tournament final.Alcaraz went on to beat Casper Ruud 7-5, 6-4 in the Miami final to win his first Masters 1000 title. Afterward, the two shared an emotional moment.Their professional partnership eventually ended in December 2025 after about seven years. Even then, Alcaraz made clear how much Ferrero had meant to his career, calling their time together an important chapter of his life.The clearest proof of Alcaraz’s growth came in 2026.He entered the Australian Open without a title at Melbourne Park, but defeated Novak Djokovic in the final to win his seventh Grand Slam. That victory completed all four major titles for Alcaraz: the US Open, Wimbledon, Roland Garros and Australian Open.At 22 years and 272 days, he became the youngest man to complete the Career Grand Slam in the Open Era.His Grand Slam record now includes two US Open titles, two Wimbledon titles, two French Open titles and one Australian Open title.Even with those achievements, the idea behind the Three Cs remains easy to understand. Head is about making good decisions. Heart is about loving the game. Courage is about taking the shot when the moment demands it.That message began with his grandfather and became part of Alcaraz’s identity long before he was winning major trophies. His tattoo keeps those words close, while the years with Ferrero helped him learn how to handle the pressure that comes with becoming a champion.And now, at 23, Alcaraz is already a seven-time major winner and a Career Grand Slam champion. His records have grown, but the family lesson behind the three letters has stayed remarkably simple.

Article Title: “I was just struggling”: George Russell admits it was tough to lose the Monza win after leading for much of the race before Kimi Antonelli passed him
Article Text:

George Russell left the Italian Grand Prix with a result that was hard to fully enjoy. The Mercedes driver had controlled much of the race at Monza and looked to be on course for victory. But a late charge from teammate Kimi Antonelli changed everything, leaving Russell with second place after a race that came down to strategy, tire life and a tense fight between the two Mercedes cars.Russell had a strong start to the race and soon moved ahead of pole sitter Pierre Gasly. From there, he looked comfortable at the front while Antonelli faced a much bigger challenge.The Italian had started from 19th on the grid. Despite that difficult position, Antonelli made rapid progress through the field and soon found himself fighting near the front.The situation became even more interesting when a Virtual Safety Car was introduced after Lance Stroll's Aston Martin stopped on track.Mercedes then split its strategy.Antonelli was brought into the pits for fresh tires, while Russell remained on the circuit. The decision initially sent Antonelli backward, but the fresher tires gave him an important advantage for the closing stages.Russell said he had expected a different approach from Mercedes.“To be honest I thought we were both going to stay out. I was surprised to see him pit,” he said.As the race moved toward its final laps, Russell began to struggle with his tires. He had stayed out on the same hard tire, leaving him with less grip as Antonelli closed the gap.“I was just struggling with the tyres towards the end,” Russell explained.Antonelli eventually got close enough to make his move. With only a few laps left, he passed Russell and took control of the race.The Italian then held on to win at his home circuit, while Russell finished second.For Russell, it was a frustrating way to lose a race he had led for so long. Still, he recognized how quickly the balance had shifted.Russell could have easily focused on the disappointment of losing the victory. Instead, he gave credit to Mercedes for taking a calculated risk.The split strategy meant one driver would benefit if the fresh tires proved decisive, while the other had track position. There was no guarantee which approach would work better.“I think at the end it was a roll of the dice both ways,” Russell said.He also explained that the team could not have known for certain which choice would produce the better result.“In the moment, the team wouldn't have known which strategy was better. It made sense to split the cars but, in the end, Kimi had great pace, and there we are.”That final point was important. Antonelli did not simply benefit from the strategy. He still had to use the opportunity, and his pace allowed him to catch and pass Russell before the checkered flag.Russell was quick to praise his teammate.“Huge congratulations to Kimi of course, an incredible result from him,” he said.The victory was especially significant for Antonelli because it came at his home race after starting from the back of the field.Russell, meanwhile, was left with the feeling that second place was still a step in the right direction after a difficult period.“I'll take it, it's been more positive than it was pre-summer break and that's what I needed to try and achieve,” he said.There was still no hiding what he wanted most.“Of course I would have loved to be P1 today.”The result extended Antonelli's Drivers' Championship lead to 66 points, while Russell strengthened his position in second ahead of Lewis Hamilton.Monza therefore delivered two very different outcomes for Mercedes. Antonelli celebrated a dream home victory, while Russell had to accept that his teammate and a different tire strategy had turned a likely win into another podium.

NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan star cricketer Mohammad Yousuf has said the country's current cricket crisis began after their famous 10-wicket win over India at the 2021 T20 World Cup in Dubai.Pakistan had never beaten India in a World Cup before that match. Babar Azam scored an unbeaten 68, while Mohammad Rizwan made 79 not out as Pakistan chased down 152 without losing a wicket. The win was celebrated as a historic moment for Pakistan cricket.However, Yousuf believes the victory also changed the mindset of the players and played a role in the team's decline in the years that followed.Yousuf said the players became too confident after beating India and failed to understand what they needed to do next.“That match which we won against India in 2021, that damaged us a lot. Because after that victory, players started to think that they had achieved something big. They couldn’t understand what they had to do next. When you are performing well, you should stay humble. If you behave with your collar raised, and get disrespectful, problems will arrive. And a lot of them have arrived in Pakistan cricket,” said Yousuf in a conversation on Samaa TV.Yousuf believes the problem was not only about Pakistan's results. He feels the team's attitude also changed after the famous win.Yousuf also blamed the fight for captaincy for some of Pakistan's problems.He said players became more interested in becoming the team's captain instead of taking responsibility for their performances.“Everyone in the team was trying to become the captain of the Pakistan team. The consequences are still hurting Pakistan cricket. Look at all the cricket Pakistan has played in the last four-five years, from ODI World Cups, T20 World Cups to Asia Cups and Champions Trophy. There has been terrible cricket. The PCB has been supporting you throughout. So many coaches have come and gone, so many things have changed just to try and help the Pakistan team. But no player has stood up and taken responsibility. Eventually, PCB had to take a step that it did. I back what PCB did,” added Yousuf.Yousuf's comments have come at a difficult time for Pakistan cricket. The team suffered heavy defeats in the first two Tests against England. Pakistan lost the Headingley Test by an innings and 103 runs before suffering a 194-run defeat at Lord's. The Pakistan Cricket Board then made major changes in the middle of the England tour.Seven players - Mohammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman, Khurram Shahzad, Aamir Jamal and Muhammad Awais Jafar - were sent back to Pakistan with one Test still left in the series.The PCB also removed head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant coach Umar Gul. Seven replacements were called up, including five uncapped players.The decision to make major changes in the middle of a Test series attracted a lot of attention. However, Yousuf said he had no problem with the PCB's decision.When asked whether the board was right to take action with one Test still remaining, he said: “Yes, there is no issue with when PCB have taken action. The Pakistan team is ninth in the World Test Championship standings. They are ninth because there are only nine teams in the table. Pakistan ka naam kharab ho raha hai (Pakistan’s reputation is getting ruined). So when that’s happening, the board has to take some steps to improve. ”Yousuf also suggested that something may have happened inside the dressing room that led to the seven players being sent home.Yousuf said Pakistan's problems cannot be blamed only on the ongoing England series.He pointed to the team's poor performances in major tournaments over the last few years.“I don’t see an issue with the PCB reaction. Because the team has been playing terrible cricket. It’s not just this one series against England. We played in the T20 World Cup final in 2022 and played in an Asia Cup final as well, but since those finals, just look at the performances coming out of this Pakistan team,” Yousuf said.Pakistan have struggled across formats in recent years. They were swept 2-0 by Bangladesh earlier this year, their second 0-2 series defeat against the same opposition after the 2024 home series.The team's poor performances have raised questions over its leadership, selection and overall direction.But for Yousuf, the root of the problem goes back to that famous night in Dubai in 2021, when Pakistan finally beat India by 10 wickets in a World Cup match.
Article Summary: Yousuf says pakistan's current cricket crisis began after their famous 10-wicket win over india at the 2021 t20 world cup in dubai. He believes the victory also changed the mindset of the players and played a role in the team's decline in the years that followed. Yousuf also blamed the fight for captaincy for some of pakistan's problems.
